# Line

```{r}
#| include: false
source("../R/setup.R")
```

How did one value change over time? `line` sorts the rows by `x`, from
smallest to largest, and draws one stroke through their `(x, y)` points in that
order, the **x order**. The stroke is straight pieces laid end to end, each
joining one row's point to the next, with nothing smoothed between them.

## Basic usage {#basic-usage}

How did life expectancy change in five Asian countries? The `gapminder_asia`
table holds China, India, Indonesia, Japan and South Korea (`Korea, Rep.` in the table), with one row for
each country every five years from 1952 to 2007. Most examples in this chapter
start from the smallest sentence that draws a line: a source, the mark, and its
two positions.

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(gapminder_asia)
```

```{r}
#| message: true
data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(year) + y(life)
```

*"Given gapminder Asia: a line, x is year, y is life."*

The stroke looks wrong, but gog drew exactly what the sentence asks for. All
five countries have a
row for each year, so the one stroke passes through five values at every year.
The vertical segments are where it joins the five countries inside one year,
before it continues to the next year. That is exactly what a line does when nothing
splits the rows: it draws one **series**, a single stroke in x order. Above the
plot, gog prints a message that names what to add: a `color` or a `group` for
several series, or `line * mean` for one value at each year. That value is the
average life expectancy of the five countries in that year, so the line shows
how their average changed over the years.
[Multiple series](#multiple-series), two sections below,
draws the same table as five lines, one per country.

## Automatic sorting by x {#automatic-sorting-by-x}

The rows of a table can be in any order: a file may be sorted by name, or by
nothing at all. `line` sorts its own vertices, the points it joins, by `x`, so
the order of the rows does not matter. The `scrambled` table holds five years
and a life expectancy for each, listed out of order on purpose. The line still
runs from left to right:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(scrambled)
```

```{r}
data(scrambled) + line + x(year) + y(life)
```

*"Given scrambled: a line, x is year, y is life."*

That sorting is part of what the mark means. It is not an extra step that the
engine performs for you. A line says *this value changed along this axis*, and
an axis has one direction, so there is only one order the vertices could be
joined in.

[`path`](path.qmd) is the mark that does the opposite. It joins the rows in the
order your table holds them, which is what draws a route or a loop. Here is the
`scrambled` table drawn both ways, with a point at each row:

```{r}
(data(scrambled) + line + point + x(year) + y(life) + title("line")) |
  (data(scrambled) + path + point + x(year) + y(life) + title("path"))
```

*"Given scrambled: a line, and also points, x is year, y is life, beside a path,
and also points, x is year, y is life."*

The line joins the five points from left to right. The path starts at 1992,
the first row, and goes to 1962, 2002, 1972 and 1982 in turn, so it runs back
and forth and crosses itself. So choosing between the two is choosing whether
the order of your rows carries meaning. With `line` the row order cannot carry
meaning; with `path` the row order sets the whole shape.

## Multiple series {#multiple-series}

The chapter's first plot drew one stroke through all five countries, and gog
asked for a `color` or a `group`. Here is the same table with `color(country)`
added in the upper plot and `group(country)` in the lower one. Both split the
single stroke into a line per country:

```{r}
(data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(year) + y(life) + color(country) +
   title("color(country)")) /
  (data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(year) + y(life) + group(country) +
     title("group(country)"))
```

*"Given gapminder Asia: lines, x is year, y is life, color by country, above
lines, x is year, y is life, grouped by country."*

Each unique value in `country` becomes a separate line in both. `color` does two
things at once. It splits the rows into one line per country, and it paints
each line its own color, with a legend, so you can tell which line belongs to
which country. [`group`](../channels.qmd#group) does only the first: the lines
in the lower plot are split, all in one color, and no legend is drawn. Use it when the overall pattern of the lines matters and the name of
each line does not, as in the [Many groups](../cookbook/groups.qmd#grouping-without-a-legend)
recipe.

## Layering a line over other marks {#layering-a-line-over-other-marks}

A line shows the trend and hides where the measurements were. A dot at each
row shows them again, which is why `line` and `point` are so often combined.
Where you write `color` decides which of the two it colors. Written *before*
the marks, it belongs to the plot, so both layers use it. Written after a mark,
it belongs to that mark alone ([Which marks a channel
reaches](../grammar.qmd#which-marks-a-channel-reaches)). The three plots below
show each place. Outside the outer parentheses,
[`theme(height = 900)`](../style.qmd#theme-settings-that-belong-to-no-mark)
sets the height of the whole figure, so each of the three plots has room:

```{r}
((data(gapminder_asia) + x(year) + y(life) + color(country) + line + point +
    title("color(country) before the marks")) /
   (data(gapminder_asia) + x(year) + y(life) + line + color(country) + point +
      title("color(country) after line")) /
   (data(gapminder_asia) + x(year) + y(life) + line + group(country) + point +
      color(country) + title("color(country) after point"))) +
  theme(height = 900)
```

*"Given gapminder Asia: x is year, y is life, color by country, lines and also
points, above x is year, y is life, lines colored by country, and also points,
above x is year, y is life, lines grouped by country, and also points colored
by country."*

In the top plot, the lines and the points share one color per country. In the
middle plot, `color(country)` follows `line`, so only the lines are colored. In
the bottom plot, it follows `point`, so it splits and colors only the points. The
line is split by `group(country)`, written after `line`, which splits without
coloring. A
layer that takes no `color` is drawn in dark gray whenever the plot has a color
legend, so it cannot be mistaken for a country ([Channels: plot-scoped or
layer-scoped](../encoding-scope.qmd#channels-plot-scoped-or-layer-scoped)).

The bottom plot uses `color` and `group` together, and it shows what each one is
for:

| Channel | Splits the rows | Colors each group | Draws a legend |
|---|---|---|---|
| `color(country)` | yes | yes | yes |
| `group(country)` | yes | no | no |

So write `color` on the layer that should show which country is which, and
`group` on any other layer that has to be split the same way. Here the points
carry the colors and the legend. The line is split by `group`, so it does not
zigzag through all five countries, as the chapter's first plot did.

### Giving each layer its own appearance {#giving-each-layer-its-own-appearance}

You do not have to map a column to `color` at all. Sometimes you want one color
for the lines and another for the points, chosen by you rather than read from
the data. That is a *setting*, written `style(color = )`, and no legend appears.
`group(country)` still keeps one line per country: it splits without coloring.
A `style()` applies only to the nearest mark before it, so each layer can be
styled on its own:

```{r}
data(gapminder_asia) + x(year) + y(life) +
  line + group(country) + style(color = "steelblue") +
  point + style(color = "firebrick", size = 3) +
  title("Blue line, red points: styled per layer")
```

*"Given gapminder Asia: x is year, y is life, lines grouped by country, colored
steelblue, and also points, colored firebrick, with size 3."*

A channel can belong to the whole plot or to one layer. Written before any mark,
it belongs to the plot and reaches every layer, as `color(country)` did above.
Written after a mark, it belongs to that mark alone, like `style()`, so each
layer can map a different column. The whole rule, for every atom, is one table
in [Encoding scope](../encoding-scope.qmd#the-rule):

```{r}
data(gapminder_asia) + x(year) + y(life) +
  line  + color(country) +
  point + size(population) +
  title("Color on the lines, size on the points")
```

*"Given gapminder Asia: x is year, y is life, lines colored by country, and also
points sized by population."*

Each layer maps its own column here: `color(country)` reaches only the lines,
and `size(population)` only the points.

## A category on the domain: the profile {#a-category-on-the-domain-the-profile}

In [Point](point.qmd#either-axis-a-horizontal-strip), swapping the two bindings
turned a strip plot on its side. Whether a swap turns a line depends on its
columns, because a line's two axes have two different jobs. One is the
**domain**, the axis the line is read along. The other is the
**measure**, the quantity it traces.

A bar draws horizontally when you swap its bindings, because the axis that holds
its categorical column is the axis that holds the slots. A line reads its domain
the same way when it has a categorical column: the category is always the
domain. But a line's two columns are usually both numbers, such as year and
life, and then nothing in the columns says which one to read along. So with two
numbers, the domain is always `x`. The
`quarterly` table, despite its name, holds one sales figure for each year. With
the years on `x`, the line is the plot you expect:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(quarterly)
```

```{r}
data(quarterly) + line + x(year) + y(sales) +
  title("Years on x: sales read along the years")
```

*"Given quarterly: a line, x is year, y is sales."*

Sales climbed for most of the years. They fell in 2008 and 2009, and again in
2020, and rose again after each fall. Swap the two bindings and the line still
sorts along `x`, which is now sales. The stroke starts at 2009, the year with the
lowest sales. Later it climbs from 2012 to 2020 and drops back to 2013, because
2020's sales fall between those of 2012 and 2013. `tick_count = 20` on the year
axis gives it a tick for every year, so each one can be read
([`tick_count`](../scales.qmd#tick_count-how-many-ticks-the-axis-aims-for)):

```{r}
data(quarterly) + line + x(sales) + y(year, tick_count = 20) +
  title("The bindings swapped: the line still sorts along x")
```

*"Given quarterly: a line, x is sales, y is year with 20 ticks."*

The zigzag seems to show a value that rose and fell many times. It does not.
Each segment joins a year to the year with the next higher sales, not to the
next year, so the rises and falls come from the sorting. Only the overall slope
is real, and only because sales were mostly higher in later years.

So the swap has two outcomes. When both columns are numbers, the line still
sorts along `x`, and the swap draws a different picture, as above. When one
column is a category, the swap moves it to `y`, and the line is read down the
page, as [The profile, turned](#the-profile-turned) shows below.

Sometimes a continuous domain has to run up the page, as depth does in a plot of ocean
temperature, or as the years do here. Then write [`path`](path.qmd) instead. A
path joins the rows in the order the table holds them. The `quarterly` table is
sorted by year, so the path runs up the page from the first year to the last.
That is the vertical series the line could not draw:

```{r}
data(quarterly) + path + x(sales) + y(year) +
  title("The same rows, joined in table order")
```

*"Given quarterly: a path, x is sales, y is year."*

Now put a category on the domain. Connecting one summary per
category is the **profile plot**. The `gapminder_2007` table holds one row for
each of 142 countries in 2007, with its continent, life expectancy, population
and GDP per person:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(gapminder_2007)
```

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + line * mean + point * mean + x(continent) + y(life) +
  y_label("Mean life expectancy") +
  title("line * mean + x(continent): one value per category, joined")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: a line derived by mean and also points derived by mean,
x is continent, y is life."*

The `mean` transform is what makes the profile readable. Without it, a `line`
connects all 142 rows across five category slots:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + line + x(continent) + y(life) +
  title("Without the transform: 142 rows across five slots")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: a line, x is continent, y is life."*

No reader can follow that. Inside each slot the stroke runs up and down through
every country, and between slots it joins the last country of one slot to the
first country of the next. gog prints a message in your session when several
rows of one line share an `x` value. In
Africa, 52 countries share one slot. `mean` leaves exactly one point per
category, so the stroke joins five summaries instead of 142 rows.

Does the connection mean anything? That depends on your data. Nothing was
measured between Africa and the Americas, and the segment is still drawn there.
If you read only the vertices, the segments help you compare the five heights.
If you read the segments themselves, they claim a change that never happened.
gog draws what you wrote. You decide whether your data supports the
connection. When it does not, keep the `mean` and change the mark to
[`bar`](bar.qmd). A bar is in its own slot and claims nothing between one
slot and the next. An ordered category, such as a grade, a clothing size or a
survey scale, suits a line when its order is declared, because then the line
has a direction to follow. Without a declared order, gog places the categories
in the order they first appear in the rows
([Declaring the order of categories](../data.qmd#declaring-the-order-of-categories)).
Two years stored as text, in a declared order, are such a category. One line for each
country, from its value in the first year to its value in the second, is the
**slope chart** ([Comparing
categories](../cookbook/comparing.qmd#what-if-the-change-matters-most)).

Continents have no order, but a straight axis must still put one of them first
and another last. A circle has no first or last place. Drop the point layer and
add `polar()`, and the same profile is drawn around a circle. That is the **radar
chart**, and it needs no new atom:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + line * mean + x(continent) + y(life) + polar() +
  title("line * mean + polar(): the radar")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: a line derived by mean, x is continent, y is life, in
polar."*

Look at the segment from Oceania back to Asia. On the flat profile the line has
two ends, because a straight axis has two ends. In the circle the five
categories are spread around the whole ring, so the last one is beside the
first and the line closes. No atom was added to close the ring. A categorical
angular axis wraps around the circle, so a line drawn along it closes into a ring. The
[Polar](../polar.qmd) chapter covers this in full.

### The profile, turned {#the-profile-turned}

Long category names, or many categories, are easier to read down the left side
of a plot than along the bottom, as the [horizontal
strip](point.qmd#either-axis-a-horizontal-strip) showed for points. A profile
can turn the same way. Put the category on `y` and the number on `x`, and the
category is still the domain: the line joins one value per category, read from
top to bottom.

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + line * mean + point * mean + x(life) + y(continent) +
  x_label("Mean life expectancy") +
  title("line * mean + y(continent): the profile, turned")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: a line derived by mean and also points derived by mean,
x is life, y is continent."*

The five means are the ones in the profile above, and only the direction
changed. Asia, the first continent in the table, is at the top, and `mean` now
groups the rows by
`y`. [`step`](step.qmd), [`area`](area.qmd) and [`ribbon`](ribbon.qmd) turn the
same way, because a category is their domain too, on either axis.

A category on `y` turns a line even when you want the line to follow `x`. With
a rank stored as text, such as `"1st"`, on `y` and the year on `x`, the line is
read down the ranks, not along the years. [Why not
`line`?](../cookbook/comparing.qmd#why-not-line) shows those lines above the
bump chart that `path` draws instead.

A profile does not need a summary. Each line can instead follow one thing
measured several times, such as one flower through its four measurements, and
`group` names the column that says which rows belong to it.

You may know the iris data as a wide table: 150 iris flowers, 50 of each of
three species, with one row for each flower. Its species is in one column, and
its four measurements (sepal length, sepal width, petal length and petal width)
are in four more. In that table the measurements are column names, not values
in a column, so `x` cannot read them.

A profile needs a long table instead, with one row for each measurement of each
flower: `measurement` holds the name, and `cm` the value in centimeters. In the
wide table, a row was a flower. In the long table each flower has four rows, and
the `flower` column says which four belong together. You reshape a table,
turning its columns into rows, in the language you already use, as [The table
has to be tidy](../data.qmd#the-table-has-to-be-tidy) explains.
`iris_measurements` is that long table, 150 flowers in 600 rows:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(iris_measurements)
```

The last column, `standardized`, is not used in this chapter.

Both plots below color by species, and `color` splits the rows as `group` does.
But a split follows the values of one column, and `species` has three. So in the
upper plot, `color(species)` alone makes three lines. Each runs up and down
through the values of 50 flowers at every measurement, then jumps to the next
measurement. In the lower plot, `group(flower)` gives each flower its own line,
and `color` still colors it by species:

```{r}
#| message: true
((data(iris_measurements) + line + x(measurement) + y(cm) + color(species) +
    style(opacity = 0.4) + title("color(species) alone: three lines")) /
   (data(iris_measurements) + line + x(measurement) + y(cm) + color(species) +
      group(flower) + style(opacity = 0.4) +
      title("color(species) + group(flower): 150 lines"))) +
  theme(height = 800)
```

*"Given the iris measurements: lines, x is measurement, y is cm, color by
species, above the same grouped by flower."*

Above the plots, gog prints a message about the upper one, and it suggests
`group`. In the next figure, each flower is again one faint line, as in the
lower plot above. A second layer, `line * mean`, draws each species' mean profile as
a thicker line. The upper plot puts the measurements on `x`, and the lower plot
puts them on `y`:

```{r}
((data(iris_measurements) + x(measurement) + y(cm) + color(species) +
    line + group(flower) + style(opacity = 0.2) + line * mean + style(size = 3) +
    title("measurement on x: the profile across the page")) /
   (data(iris_measurements) + x(cm) + y(measurement) + color(species) +
      line + group(flower) + style(opacity = 0.2) + line * mean + style(size = 3) +
      title("measurement on y: the profile down the page"))) +
  theme(height = 900)
```

*"Given the iris measurements: x is measurement, y is cm, color by species,
lines grouped by flower, with opacity 0.2, and also lines derived by mean, with
size 3, above the same with x is cm and y is measurement."*

The two plots show the same 150 profiles. In both, the petal measurements of
*setosa* are much smaller than those of the other two species. This plot is
also called **parallel coordinates**, and [What if four or more measurements
matter
equally?](../cookbook/three-or-more.qmd#what-if-four-or-more-measurements-matter-equally)
draws it in the cookbook. A turned profile cannot be bent into a circle: in
`polar()` it is refused, as [What it refuses](#what-it-refuses) shows.

## Smoothed trend line {#smoothed-trend-line}

People in richer countries tend to live longer. The relationship between `gdp`
and `life` is positive: as one rises, the other tends to rise as well. Sometimes
the direction of a relationship is all a reader needs to know. Combine `line`
with the `smooth` transform to draw a trend line fitted through all the rows
instead of the rows themselves:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  point + color(continent) +
  line * smooth
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: x is gdp, y is life, points colored by continent, and
also a line derived by smooth."*

The point layer keeps every country visible, and `smooth` reduces the same rows
to one fitted curve. Only the `line` layer carries the transform, so the points
are untouched.

`smooth` does not average the rows at each `x` value. The `mean` transform does
that, and `line * mean` draws it. In [Basic usage](#basic-usage), five countries
share each year, so their average means something. Here each country has its own
`gdp`, so the average at each `x` would be the row itself. `smooth` computes the
curve at 100 evenly spaced places along `x` instead. At each place, it fits a
straight line through the 75% of the rows whose `x` is nearest to that place.
Nearer rows get more weight in that fit. Each fit gives one value at its place,
and the line joins those values ([`smooth`](../transforms.qmd#smooth-loess-trend-line)
has the details).

`smooth` is not only for `line`. Four other marks take it too, and each
draws the same fitted curve in its own way:

| Mark derived by `smooth` | What it draws |
|---|---|
| `point * smooth` | one dot at each fitted value |
| `area * smooth` | the curve filled to the baseline |
| `bar * smooth` | one thin bar at each fitted value |
| `step * smooth` | the curve as a staircase |
| `line * smooth` | the fitted curve above |

## A running total {#a-running-total}

A line can show how a quantity adds up over time. The
[`cumulative`](../transforms.qmd#cumulative-the-running-total) transform adds
each year's value to the years before it, so the line passes through the total
so far. The `quarterly` table, shown in [A category on the
domain](#a-category-on-the-domain-the-profile), holds one year of sales in each
row:

```{r}
data(quarterly) + line * cumulative + x(year) + y(sales) +
  title("Sales so far, since 2005")
```

*"Given quarterly: a line derived by cumulative, x is year, y is sales."*

The line ends at 2,595, the sales of all 19 years. It always rises, because the
sales of every year are positive. The rise from one year to the next is the
sales of the later year. So the flattest piece is the one that ends at 2009,
when sales fell to 88. With
`color` or `group`, each line adds up its own rows.

## Two boundaries from a pair {#two-boundaries-from-a-pair}

Sometimes the answer at each `x` is two values rather than one: a lowest and a
highest, or the spread around a mean. Most transforms compute one
value per `x`. A **pair** transform gives it two, a low and a high. A
`line` then draws *both boundaries* as two separate lines, not one zigzag
joining them. A [`ribbon`](ribbon.qmd) takes the same pair and fills the band
between the two boundaries; a line draws only the boundaries. There are six
pair transforms: [`range`](../transforms.qmd#range-a-lowhigh-pair),
[`confidence`](../transforms.qmd#confidence-the-interval-of-the-mean),
[`deviation`](../transforms.qmd#deviation-the-spread-of-the-data),
[`smooth_band`](../transforms.qmd#smooth_band-the-band-around-the-curve),
[`straight_band`](../transforms.qmd#straight_band-the-band-around-the-line) and
[`bounds`](../transforms.qmd#bounds-a-pre-computed-lowhigh-pair). The
`gapminder_asia` table, shown in [Basic usage](#basic-usage), holds five
countries. Here are the lowest and the highest life expectancy among them in
each year, drawn as two lines:

```{r}
data(gapminder_asia) + line * range + x(year) + y(life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The lowest and highest life expectancy, as two lines")
```

*"Given gapminder Asia: a line derived by range, x is year, y is life."*

Add `style(pattern = "dashed")` for the dashed band often used in published
figures. That plot is in [Ribbon](ribbon.qmd#filled-or-two-dashed-edges), which
shows the same pair filled and then as two dashed edges.

## Stroke width and opacity {#stroke-width-and-opacity}

You may want thicker lines for a slide, or fainter ones where many lines cross.
A line takes one width and one opacity for the whole layer, not one per row.
`style()` sets them:

```{r}
data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(year) + y(life) + group(country) +
  style(size = 4, opacity = 0.45) +
  title("One width, one opacity, for the whole layer")
```

*"Given gapminder Asia: lines, x is year, y is life, grouped by country, with
size 4 and opacity 0.45."*

A mapped `color` is different: it can change along one line. gog draws that
line as short segments, one color each, so the color changes at every vertex. A
width could change at every vertex in the same way, and some libraries draw
that. gog does not: it keeps one width and one opacity for the whole layer.
Mapping `gdp` to `size` is refused, and the message says to set one width
with `style(size = )`:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(year) + y(life) + group(country) + size(gdp)
```

Mapping the same column to `color` is allowed. Each country's line changes color
along its length, and the legend is a [ramp](../channels.qmd#ramps) rather than
one color per country:

```{r}
data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(year) + y(life) + group(country) +
  color(gdp, scale = "log") + palette("viridis") +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("Each country's line, colored by its income")
```

*"Given gapminder Asia: lines, x is year, y is life, grouped by country, color
by gdp on a log scale, with the viridis palette."*

Read one country's line from left to right and you see two variables. The height
is how long people live, and the color is how rich the country was then. The
width is the same along every line; only the color changes. `group` still
splits the mark into one line per country; `color` carries the second variable,
income. A *categorical* `color` splits and colors at the same time, as [Multiple
series](#multiple-series) showed above.

`palette()` chooses the colors a mapping uses. `"viridis"` is a ramp, and the
named palettes and what each is for are in [Palettes](../channels.qmd#palettes).

Two questions look alike and are not the same: *"Does this mark have this
property?"* and *"Can a column be mapped here?"* For a line's width, the first
answer is yes and the second is no. For its color, both answers are yes.
[Setting vs mapping](../style.qmd#two-questions-not-one) uses a line as its
clearest case.

Setting one pale color on a layer is the usual way to make another layer easier
to see:

```{r}
data(gapminder_asia) + x(year) + y(life) +
  line + group(country) + style(color = "lightgray") +
  line * smooth + style(color = "firebrick", size = 3) +
  title("Every country in gray, the trend in red")
```

*"Given gapminder Asia: x is year, y is life, lines grouped by country, colored
lightgray, and also a line derived by smooth, colored firebrick, with size 3."*

Each layer here carries its own `style()`. A `style()` applies only to the
nearest mark before it, and to no other mark. The first one colors the five
country lines light gray, and the second colors and thickens only the trend. The
first one does not reach the trend: without the second, the trend would be
drawn in the default blue. Unlike a channel, `style()` cannot belong to the
whole plot. Written before any mark, it is refused, because it has no mark to
style. In [`style` and the layer it
follows](../style.qmd#style-and-the-layer-it-follows), only the points have a
`style()`, and the trend line keeps its default color.

## Each country and its continent's mean or median {#each-country-and-its-continents-mean-or-median}

The plot above draws five countries and one trend. The `gm_all` table holds 142
countries, measured every five years from 1952 to 2007. In one panel, 142 gray
lines are too many to read. One trend through all of them would also hide how
the continents differ. So draw one panel for each continent, with its countries
in gray and their mean as one blue line.

The sentence below has two `line` layers. The first draws one gray line for each
country, as above. The second is `line * mean`. In each year, `mean` averages
the values of the countries, so it leaves one value per year, and the line joins
those values. `| facet(continent)` splits the whole plot into one panel per
continent. Every layer is split the same way, so the blue line in each panel is
the mean of that continent's countries. [Faceting](../faceting.qmd) explains the
operator in full.

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(gm_all)
```

```{r}
data(gm_all) + x(year) + y(life) +
  line + group(country) + style(color = "lightgray") +
  line * mean + style(color = "steelblue", size = 3) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Every country, and the continent's mean") | facet(continent)
```

*"Given all the gapminder years: x is year, y is life, lines grouped by country,
and also a line derived by mean, split into panel columns by continent."*

The blue line is the continent's mean, and the gray lines show how far each
country was from it. Every continent's mean rose over the whole period, but Africa's
stopped rising for fifteen years. It rose from 39 years in 1952 to 53 in 1987, and in 2002 it
was still 53. In 22 of Africa's 52 countries, life expectancy was lower in 2002
than in 1987. In Zimbabwe it fell from 62 years to 40. The table has only two
countries in Oceania, Australia and New Zealand, so the blue line almost covers
their two gray lines.

`smooth` summarizes the same rows another way. Instead of averaging the
countries in each year, it fits a curve to each continent's rows, as [Smoothed
trend line](#smoothed-trend-line) describes:

```{r}
data(gm_all) + x(year) + y(life) +
  line + group(country) + style(color = "lightgray") +
  line * smooth + style(color = "firebrick", size = 3) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Every country, and the continent's smooth trend") | facet(continent)
```

*"Given all the gapminder years: x is year, y is life, lines grouped by country,
and also a line derived by smooth, split into panel columns by continent."*

In four of the five panels, the red curve has nearly the same shape as the blue
line in the previous plot, because those means rise at a nearly steady rate. In
Africa they differ. The `mean` line stops rising after 1987 and falls a little in
2002. The red curve only rises more slowly, so it hides the stop. The `mean`
line passes through each of the 12 yearly averages, so it shows every change of
direction. Each point of the `smooth` curve is fitted from the rows of the nine
nearest of the 12 years. Those nine years cover a period of 40 years, so a stop
of 15 years becomes a gentle bend.

Use `mean` when you want the average at each `x` value, with every change in it.
It needs many rows at each value, as here, where every country has a row for
each year. Use `smooth` when you want the general direction, or when no two rows
share an `x` value, as in [Smoothed trend line](#smoothed-trend-line).

Income is a second way to compare the continents. The two layers of the `mean`
plot can draw GDP per person, with two changes to the sentence. The first change is the scale.
GDP per person runs from a few hundred dollars to more than a hundred thousand,
so the next plot draws it on a log scale. On this scale each labeled tick is ten
times the one below it, so the poorer countries are not crowded together at the
bottom.

The second change is the summary. gog computes `mean` in dollars, and only then
places the result on the log axis ([The measured value keeps its own
units](../scales.qmd#the-measured-value-keeps-its-own-units)). In dollars, one
very rich country can raise the mean far above most of the others. In 1952,
Kuwait's GDP per person was 108,382 dollars, and Asia's mean was 5,195. Sorted
from poorest to richest, the middle one of Asia's 33 countries had 1,207, less
than a quarter of the mean. In the Asia panel, a mean line would therefore run
above most of the gray lines. The
[`median`](../transforms.qmd#aggregation-family-sum-mean-median-max-min-quantile)
is that middle value, and sorting the countries gives the same order in dollars
as in logarithms. So `line * median` has half of the gray lines above it and
half below, on a log axis too:

```{r}
data(gm_all) + x(year) + y(gdp, scale = "log") +
  line + group(country) + style(color = "lightgray") +
  line * median + style(color = "steelblue", size = 3) +
  y_label("GDP per person") +
  title("GDP per person on five continents") | facet(continent)
```

*"Given all the gapminder years: x is year, y is gdp on a log scale, lines
grouped by country, and also a line derived by median, split into panel columns
by continent."*

The medians grew at very different rates. Europe's rose from 5,142 dollars in
1952 to 28,054 in 2007, more than five times its 1952 value. Africa's rose from
987 dollars to 1,452, less than one and a half times its 1952 value. In 2002 it
was lower than in 1972.

## Transforms it takes {#transforms-it-takes}

A transform computes new values from the rows, and the mark draws those values
instead of the rows. The table lists, by kind, the transforms a line takes and
the ones it refuses:

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
mark_transforms("line")
```

The plots below show every transform a line takes. Within a figure the plots
differ mainly in their transform, and the paragraph before each figure names any
other change.

**Counting.** `count` and `proportion` tally the rows at each value of `x`, on a
category or a number. `bin` and `density` work on a number. `bin` counts the
rows in each interval, and `density` estimates, as a smooth curve, how closely
the rows lie along the axis. Each puts its result on the axis you leave empty,
and the line joins the results in order along `x`. With `bin`, the stroke passes
through the center of each bin, and the plot is called a **frequency polygon**.
The top two plots put `continent` on `x`, and the plot below them puts `life`:

```{r}
((data(gapminder_2007) + line * count + x(continent) + title("line * count")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + line * proportion + x(continent) +
     title("line * proportion"))) /
  (data(gapminder_2007) + line * bin + x(life) + title("line * bin"))
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: a line derived by count, x is continent, beside a line
derived by proportion, x is continent; above a line derived by bin, x is life."*

The density is drawn in a figure of its own. In one figure with the `bin` plot,
the two would share one `life` axis that covers only the range of the rows, and
the density's tails would be cut off ([A plot cut by a shared
axis](../composition.qmd#a-plot-cut-by-a-shared-axis)). `line * density` draws the
estimated curve as one stroke:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + line * density + x(life) + title("line * density")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: a line derived by density, x is life."*

Look at the `y` axis of the four plots above, from `line * count` to
`line * density`. None of the four sentences writes `y()`, yet each `y` axis has
a name: Count, Proportion, Count and Density. The table has no column by those
names. Each transform writes one, and `y` draws it. `count` and `bin` write
`count`, the number of rows at each value or in each interval. `proportion`
writes `proportion`, each count's share of all the rows. `density` writes
`density`, the height of the estimated curve. The axis is labeled with the
column's name, capitalized, as [The name on a measure
axis](../transforms.qmd#the-name-on-a-measure-axis) explains.

The two plots on top have the same shape, because each proportion is a count
divided by 142, the number of countries. In those two plots, read only the
vertices. Nothing was measured between two continents, as [A category on the
domain](#a-category-on-the-domain-the-profile) explains.

**Summaries.** The six summaries reduce the rows at each value of `x` to one
value, so they need a number on `y`. The `gm_all` table, shown in [Each
country and its continent's mean or
median](#each-country-and-its-continents-mean-or-median), has 142 rows for each
year, one for each country. That section draws the `mean` and `median` lines
of each continent. Each line below joins one value for each year.
`sum` reads `population`, because only an amount has a total that means
something. The other five read `life`. They give the mean, the median, the
largest and the smallest value, and `quantile(0.9)` gives the value that nine
tenths of the rows fall below:

```{r}
((data(gm_all) + line * sum + x(year) + y(population) +
    title("line * sum")) |
  (data(gm_all) + line * mean + x(year) + y(life) +
     title("line * mean")) |
  (data(gm_all) + line * median + x(year) + y(life) +
     title("line * median"))) /
  ((data(gm_all) + line * max + x(year) + y(life) +
      title("line * max")) |
     (data(gm_all) + line * min + x(year) + y(life) +
        title("line * min")) |
     (data(gm_all) + line * quantile(0.9) + x(year) + y(life) +
        title("line * quantile(0.9)")))
```

*"Given all the gapminder years: a line derived by sum, x is year, y is
population, beside a line derived by mean, x is year, y is life, beside a line
derived by median, x is year, y is life; above a line derived by max, x is year,
y is life, beside a line derived by min, x is year, y is life, beside a line
derived by quantile at 0.9, x is year, y is life."*

The five plots that read `life` share one scale, so their heights can be
compared from plot to plot. Only `min` falls as well as rises. It falls twice:
from 35.4 years in 1972 to Cambodia's 31.2 in 1977, and from 39.9 years in 1987
to Rwanda's 23.6 in 1992.

**Fitted lines.** `smooth` and `straight` need a number on each axis. They fit a
line to the rows, each placed at its `x` and its `y`. `smooth` follows the
shape of the data, and `straight` is the least-squares line. Each fit gives a
value at evenly spaced places along `x`, 100 unless you set `places`, and the
line joins those values into one stroke. [Smoothed trend
line](#smoothed-trend-line) draws `smooth` over the countries and says how it
fits, and [Each country and its continent's mean or
median](#each-country-and-its-continents-mean-or-median) compares it with
`mean`.

**Running total.** `cumulative` adds each value to the ones before it along the
axis. The third plot reads the `quarterly` table, shown in [A category on the
domain](#a-category-on-the-domain-the-profile), with `year` on `x` and `sales`
on `y`. It is the plot in [A running total](#a-running-total), drawn again here
beside the fits:

```{r}
((data(gapminder_2007) + line * smooth + x(gdp) + y(life) +
    title("line * smooth")) |
   (data(gapminder_2007) + line * straight + x(gdp) + y(life) +
      title("line * straight")) |
   (data(quarterly) + line * cumulative + x(year) + y(sales) +
      title("line * cumulative"))) +
  theme(height = 450)
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: a line derived by smooth, x is gdp, y is life, beside a
line derived by straight, x is gdp, y is life; beside a line from quarterly,
derived by cumulative, x is year, y is sales."*

**Pairs.** The pair transforms give `y` a low and a high at each value of `x`,
and a line draws each of the two as its own stroke. `range`, `confidence` and
`deviation` read a number on `y`, and like the summaries they reduce the rows at
each value of `x`. `range` gives the smallest and the largest value, as in
[Two boundaries from a pair](#two-boundaries-from-a-pair), which draws it for
five countries.
`confidence` gives the confidence interval of the mean, at 95% unless you name
another level. `deviation` reaches one standard deviation from the mean on each
side, unless you name another number. Both also compute the mean itself, which
a line leaves out:

```{r}
((data(gm_all) + line * range + x(year) + y(life) + title("line * range")) |
   (data(gm_all) + line * confidence + x(year) + y(life) +
      title("line * confidence")) |
   (data(gm_all) + line * deviation + x(year) + y(life) +
      title("line * deviation"))) +
  theme(height = 450)
```

*"Given all the gapminder years: a line derived by range, x is year, y is life,
beside a line derived by confidence, x is year, y is life, beside a line derived
by deviation, x is year, y is life."*

The two lines of `confidence` differ by about 4 years of life expectancy in every
year, because the mean of 142 values varies little. The two lines of `deviation`
differ by 21 to 25 years, because they show how far the countries spread.

Some reports use a 99% interval, or lines two standard deviations from the mean.
Write the number in parentheses after the transform's name. `confidence` takes
the confidence level, a number greater than 0 and less than 1, so 0.95 rather
than 95. It is 0.95 when you leave it
out, and `confidence(0.99)` draws the 99% interval. Below, the default pair is
drawn in blue and the other pair in red:

```{r}
data(gm_all) + line * confidence + x(year) + y(life) +
  style(color = "steelblue") +
  line * confidence(0.99) + style(color = "firebrick") +
  title("confidence: 95% in blue, 99% in red")
```

*"Given all the gapminder years: a line derived by confidence, x is year, y is
life, colored steelblue, and also a line derived by confidence at 99%, colored
firebrick."*

The two pairs share a center, the mean, and the red pair is wider. The red
lines differ by about 5 years, and the blue lines by about 4. A 95% interval
contains the population mean in 95 of every 100 samples, and a 99% interval in
99, so it is wider.

`deviation` takes the number of standard deviations on each side of the mean. It
is 1 when you leave it out, and `deviation(2)` reaches two:

```{r}
data(gm_all) + line * deviation + x(year) + y(life) +
  style(color = "steelblue") +
  line * deviation(2) + style(color = "firebrick") +
  title("deviation in blue, deviation(2) in red")
```

*"Given all the gapminder years: a line derived by deviation, x is year, y is
life, colored steelblue, and also a line derived by deviation at 2 standard
deviations, colored firebrick."*

The red lines differ by 42 to 49 years, twice the 21 to 25 years of the blue
lines. The Transforms chapter explains both numbers further, in its sections on
[`confidence`](../transforms.qmd#confidence-the-interval-of-the-mean) and
[`deviation`](../transforms.qmd#deviation-the-spread-of-the-data).

The other three pairs do not reduce the rows at each value of `x`. `smooth_band`
and `straight_band` fit the same line as `smooth` and `straight`, and give a low
and a high around it at the same evenly spaced places along `x`: the 95%
confidence interval of the fitted line, which shows how precisely the line is
known there. Like those two,
they need a number on
each axis. `bounds` computes nothing: it reads the low and the high from two
columns you name, and it needs no `y`. It is how a band from a statistical model
reaches a plot. gog fits only a few lines itself, while the modeling packages of
R, Python and Julia compute many kinds of interval, such as a prediction
interval or a Bayesian credible interval. Keep the lower and the upper bound as
two columns of the table, and `bounds` draws them, as
[`bounds`](../transforms.qmd#bounds-a-pre-computed-lowhigh-pair) shows. The
third plot reads the `score_band`
table, with `score` on `x`. It holds a low and a high for each raw score on a
test scored from 0 to 20, computed before the plot, so gog only draws them:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(score_band)
```

```{r}
((data(gapminder_2007) + line * smooth_band + x(gdp) + y(life) +
    title("line * smooth_band")) |
   (data(gapminder_2007) + line * straight_band + x(gdp) + y(life) +
      title("line * straight_band")) |
   (data(score_band) + line * bounds(lower, upper) + x(score) +
      title("line * bounds"))) +
  theme(height = 450)
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: a line derived by smooth_band, x is gdp, y is life,
beside a line derived by straight_band, x is gdp, y is life; beside a line from
the score band, from lower to upper, x is score."*

A line refuses every transform in the Refuses column above. The collision
modifiers move marks that would be drawn on top of one another, such as
[`bar`](bar.qmd) and [`point`](point.qmd). A line is a thin stroke, so two lines
that meet cross instead. To pile one series on another, use `stack` with
[`area`](area.qmd). `repel` moves only [`text`](text.qmd) labels.
`partition`, `flow` and `cluster` lay out rectangles, bands and branches, which
[`zone`](zone.qmd), [`ribbon`](ribbon.qmd) and [`path`](path.qmd) draw.
`layout` places a network, which [`point`](point.qmd), [`text`](text.qmd) and [`edge`](edge.qmd) draw.

## What you can set {#what-you-can-set}

A setting changes how the stroke looks without reading a column, and each
mark takes its own. [Setting vs mapping](../style.qmd) shows how a setting differs from mapping a
column. These are a line's settings, with the values each accepts:

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
mark_options("line")
```

A line is a stroke, so `size` sets its width and `pattern` sets whether it is
solid, dashed, dotted, dotdash or longdash. A setting
gives the whole layer one value. A channel reads a column instead, so what is
drawn follows the data.

Two of the four settings in the list above, `color` and `pattern`, are also channels.
`color(country)` draws one color per country. A mapped `pattern` gives each
series its own stroke pattern instead. `pattern` has five values for a stroke, including solid. gog
assigns them in the order the categories first appear in the table, and this
plot shows that order:

```{r}
stroke_patterns <- data.frame(
  stroke_pattern = c("solid", "solid", "dashed", "dashed", "dotted", "dotted",
                     "dotdash", "dotdash", "longdash", "longdash"),
  at             = c(1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 2),
  level          = c(5, 5, 4, 4, 3, 3, 2, 2, 1, 1)
)
data(stroke_patterns) + line + x(at) + y(level) + pattern(stroke_pattern) +
  style(size = 2) + x_label("") + y_label("") + title("The five stroke patterns")
```

*"Given the stroke patterns table: lines, x is at, y is level, pattern by stroke
pattern, with size 2."*

A sixth series gets the first of the five again, and gog says so: see
[`pattern`](../channels.qmd#pattern). `opacity` and `size` can only be set: a
line takes one width and one opacity for the whole layer, not one per row.
`color` is different. Of the four, only `color` can be mapped to a continuous
column, and the color then changes along a single line. [Stroke width and
opacity](#stroke-width-and-opacity) shows this after a refused `size`.

Set `size` and `pattern` together, and every series takes the same width and the
same dash. The plot reads the `gapminder_asia` table, shown in [Basic
usage](#basic-usage):

```{r}
data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(year) + y(life) + color(country) +
  style(size = 3, pattern = "dashed") +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("One width and one dash, for every series")
```

*"Given gapminder Asia: lines, x is year, y is life, color by country, with size
3 and pattern dashed."*

Each property takes its value from one source: a column, or you. Here `color`
reads a column, and `size` and `pattern` are set, so no property is given a
value twice. Ask for both on one property and gog refuses, rather than dropping
one in silence.
[Setting vs mapping](../style.qmd#mapping-and-setting-the-same-property)
shows the refusal.

A transform's own arguments are neither a mapping nor a setting. They change
what is computed, not how it is drawn. `line * density(adjust = 1.5)` widens the
bandwidth, so the curve is smoother than the default one.
[Choosing the bandwidth](../transforms.qmd#choosing-the-bandwidth) draws a
density line twice as smooth. The [Transforms](../transforms.qmd) chapter
lists what each transform takes.

The [grid of every mark and every setting](../style.qmd#what-you-can-set) shows
which other marks share this list. What a mark *maps* rather than sets is its
row on the [grid of marks and channels](../combinations.qmd#marks-and-channels).

## What it refuses {#what-it-refuses}

A line takes only the stroke patterns. `"hatch"` is a fill texture, and a line
has no area to fill.

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(year) + y(life) + style(pattern = "hatch")
```

The refusal lists the five values `pattern` does take on a stroke. Five more
refusals follow from this chapter's rules. The first is a [turned
profile](#the-profile-turned) in `polar()`. Bent into a circle, its measure
would run around the circle and its categories out along the radius, which is
not the radar. The message says that a profile turned that way does not bend
into `polar()`, and it writes the radar's sentence instead, with the category
on `x`:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_2007) + line * mean + x(life) + y(continent) + polar()
```

The second is a category on both axes. A line traces a value across its
categories, so one axis must hold a continuous column, and with categories on
both there is
nothing to trace:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_2007) + line + x(continent) + y(country)
```

The third is a line drawn over horizontal bars in one plot. A date on `y` draws
a bar horizontally, because [a bar never measures a
date](../scales.qmd#bars-on-a-date-axis). But only a category
[turns](#the-profile-turned) a line, so the line still joins its points in order
of `x`. One plot is read in one direction. The `six_weeks` table holds 42 days
of `orders`, with `day` stored as a date:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(six_weeks)
```

```{r}
#| error: true
data(six_weeks) + bar + line + x(orders) + y(day)
```

gog draws each layer alone, as the top two plots below show. The bars are
horizontal, one for each day. The line joins the same days in order of
`x(orders)`, from left to right, so it jumps up and down the date axis. In one
plot, you would read the bars up the page and the line across it.

The message names three fixes. The top two plots are the last of them, two
plots side by side with `|`, and the bottom two draw the others. With the dates
on `x`, the bars and the line are both drawn upright. To keep the bars
horizontal, join their outer ends with [`path`](path.qmd) instead of a line. A
path joins the rows in the order the table holds them. `six_weeks` is sorted by
`day`, so the path runs up the page from the first day to the last.

```{r}
((data(six_weeks) + bar + x(orders) + y(day) + title("bar alone: horizontal")) |
   (data(six_weeks) + line + x(orders) + y(day) +
      title("line alone: joined left to right, not by day"))) /
  ((data(six_weeks) + bar + line + x(day) + y(orders) +
      title("the dates on x: both upright")) |
     (data(six_weeks) + bar + path + x(orders) + y(day) +
        title("path: the bars' ends, day by day"))) +
  theme(height = 800)
```

*"Given the six weeks table: bars, x is orders, y is day, beside a line, x is
orders, y is day; above bars, and also a line, x is day, y is orders, beside
bars, and also a path, x is orders, y is day."*

The fourth is a column mapped to `size` or `opacity`. A line takes one width and
one opacity for the whole layer, not one per row. [Stroke width and
opacity](#stroke-width-and-opacity) shows this refusal before the `color`
mapping that is allowed, and it is shown again here:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_asia) + line + x(year) + y(life) + group(country) + size(gdp)
```

One last refusal concerns the series themselves. A line needs at least two
positions in each series, because a stroke runs from one position to the next.
The profile in [A category on the domain](#a-category-on-the-domain-the-profile)
joins five means. Drop its point layer and color the line by continent:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_2007) + line * mean + x(continent) + y(life) + color(continent)
```

Each continent is now a series that holds one mean, so nothing would be drawn,
and gog refuses the sentence. A split from `color`, `group`, `pattern`, `facet`
or `play` is refused in the same way, when it leaves one position in every
series and no other layer draws. When only some series hold one position, gog
draws the others and prints a message naming the ones it left out. Add `point`
with the line's transform, such as `point * mean`, and those positions are
drawn as well, as in [Layering a line over other
marks](#layering-a-line-over-other-marks).

## In short {#in-short}

A categorical `color`, a `group` or a mapped `pattern` splits the rows into one
line per category. Each line needs at least two positions. Without a split, one
stroke joins every row. A line sorts along its domain, so row order means
nothing to it. A category is the domain on either axis, and with two numbers
the domain is `x`. A line takes one width and one opacity for the whole layer,
and only `color` changes along it.

## What comes next {#what-comes-next}

You read a line by comparing its values with each other, so its axis need not
reach zero. [Bar](bar.qmd) measures from zero instead, so one bar's length has
a meaning by itself.
